annotations.annotation_text: (French) I am he.[1] Stephen's statement is a parody of the oft-quoted remark attributed to Louis XIV of France: L'état, c'est moi (I am the state).
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.target_phrase: Encore deux minutes. Look clock. Must get. Fermé
annotations.annotation_text: (French) Still two minutes to go ... Closed.[2] Stephen is recalling an incident when he tried to cash a money order from his mother at a French post-office. When the door was closed in his face, he pleaded with the usher in broken French and English: There are still two minutes to go [before closing time]. Look [at the] clock. [I] must get [this money order cashed]. To which the usher replied: [We're] closed.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).
Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.

annotations.annotation_text: et dices filiis Ammon audite verbum Domini Dei haec dicit Dominus Deus pro eo quod dixisti euge euge super sanctuarium meum quia pollutum est et super terram Israhel quoniam desolata est et super domum Iuda quoniam ducti sunt in captivitatem[4]

annotations.annotation_text: And say unto the Ammonites, Hear the word of the Lord GOD; Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou saidst, Aha, against my sanctuary, when it was profaned; and against the land of Israel, when it was desolate; and against the house of Judah, when they went into captivity;[5]
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.

annotations.annotation_text: (French) What?[7] At Newhaven in England, on his way to Paris, Stephen pretended he was French and could not speak English in order to avoid having to pay a porter threepence to carry his valise.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.annotation_text: (French) A tutu is a short ballet skirt.[8] Le Tutu was a humorous weekly magazine that first appeared in Paris on 25 March 1901.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.annotation_text: (French) White Knickers and Red Panties.[9] No such periodical is known, though the second half of the name recalls a genuine French magazine, La Vie en Culotte Rouge (Life in Red Breeches, or Among the Camp Followers).[10] It has been suggested that Joyce concocted the title so as to strengthen the link between Stephen and Bloom, for whom women's undergarments are a fetish. See 070.33 - 071.37, and of course Nausicaa.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.annotation_text: (Italian) Handsome man.[11] The Italian makes sense in the context of Trieste (see above).
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.annotation_text: (French) turnovers.[12] A chausson is a turnover made, usually, with puff pastry and a fruit filling. Chaussons aux pommes are apple turnovers.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.annotation_text: (French) pus.[13] Pus is a viscous yellowish liquid associated with bacterial infections (e.g. pimples). Stephen is referring to the yellow custard in a flan bréton.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.annotation_text: (French) custard tart.[14] In French flan denotes a baked custard tart. The variety of custard tart associated with Brittany is called a Far Breton. But Stephen's reference to the yellow pus of the custard suggests that he has some sort of custard pastry in mind in which the custard is not set, such as a mille-feuille.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4.0).

annotations.annotation_text: (French Slang) lady-killers.[16] Conquistadores is a Spanish word for the soldiers, explorers and adventurers who conquered and colonized the territories that created the Spanish Empire in the 15th-17th centuries; but the term is also used in several European languages to describe a lothario.
sources: Gifford, Don, and Robert J. Seidman. Ulysses Annotated. University of California Press, 1988.
